citation.title: The Regression Discontinuity Design under Interference: A Local Randomization-Based Approach

standing_assumptions:
The note (printed pp. 129–133 = PDF pp. 2–6; PDF p. 1 is the publisher's cover sheet) has no numbered theorem, proposition, equation or assumption and no appendix. Its one formal result is the chain of unnumbered displays on p. 131 (PDF p. 4), which rests on the model and the assumptions of p. 130 (PDF p. 3). Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
[Population and potential outcomes: Section 2, p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] “We first define our causal model and setting. Suppose we have a finite population $U$ of $N$ subjects indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ specifies which treatment value (0 = control, 1 = treatment) that subject $i$ receives. Suppose that associated with each subject $i$ are $2^N$ fixed potential outcomes, $y_i(\mathbf{z})$, defined over all $2^N$ vectors $\mathbf{z}$ such that $z_j \in \{0, 1\}, \forall j \in \{1, 2, .., N\}$. For example, $y_2\,((0, 1, 0, ..., 0))$ would represent subject 2’s potential outcome if she were treated, but no other subjects were treated. Note that this makes no assumptions about interference (or its absence): for each subject $i$, her outcome $y_i$ is allowed to depend on her own or any combination of the other subjects’ treatment statuses.”
[Assignment and observed data: p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] “To proceed, we will make assumptions about the manner in which $\mathbf{z}$ is assigned and how some potential outcomes are revealed. In particular, we will assume that $\mathbf{Z}$ is a binary random vector of length $N$. The observed data then consist of a single realization from $(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{X})$, where it is assumed that the outcome vector $\mathbf{Y} = (y_1(\mathbf{Z}), y_2(\mathbf{Z}), ..., y_N(\mathbf{Z}))$. ($\mathbf{X}$ is discussed in the following paragraph; note that potential outcomes $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ are assumed not to depend on $\mathbf{X}$.)”
[Running variable and threshold rule: p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] “Assume that associated with each subject $i$ is a random variable $X_i$ denoting the difference between subject $i$’s running variable and the threshold. We assume that whether or not a subject is treated depends solely on whether or not she is above the threshold: let $Z_i = 1$ (the subject is treated) if $X_i \geq 0$ (the subject is above the threshold), else let $Z_i = 0$ (the subject is in the control condition). In the event that we have noncompliance, let $Z_i$ instead denote treatment eligibility and all effects should be interpreted as intention-to-treat effects. The joint distribution of $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, ..., X_N)$ fully determines the joint distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$, hence knowledge of $\mathbf{X}$ implies knowledge of $\mathbf{Z}$.”
[Window: p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] “Let $b$ be the bandwidth, or the maximum distance (e.g., number of days) from the threshold at which we would still consider a subject to be close to the threshold. Denote the window $W_0 = [-b, b]$, and define the conditional distribution function $F_{\mathbf{x},W_0}$ as the empirical distribution function of $X_i$ for all subjects such that $X_i \in W_0$.”
[No ties, as printed: p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] “To simplify our definition of local randomization, without loss of generality, assume that $\Pr(X_i = X_j) = 0, \forall i, j : X_i, X_j \in W_0$, so that no two observed age values within the window are exactly identical.”
[Local randomization, as printed: p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] “Our local randomization assumption requires that $F_{\mathbf{x},W_0}(t) = F_0(t), \forall \mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$ and $\forall t$; $\Pr(X_i \in W_0) \in \{0, 1\}, \forall i \in \{1, ..., N\}$, $\Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{N_0!}, \forall \mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$, where $N_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{I}(X_i \in W_0)$: implying that all permutations of the running variable values (and therefore treatment values) within the window $W_0$ are equiprobable. Further assume that $0 < \sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Z_i < N_0$, so that at least one subject within the window is treated, and at least one subject within the window is in the control group.”
[Allocation outside the window: p. 131 (PDF p. 4)] “While the treatment allocation scheme for subjects outside of $W_0$ is left completely unspecified, the allocation scheme for these subjects nevertheless contributes to the definition of each $\overline{Y}_i(z)$. Individual average potential outcomes marginalize over the treatment assignments for all units, not simply those within the window near the threshold.”
[Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] (R1) $\mathrm{E}$ and $\Pr$ are taken over the joint law of $\mathbf{X}$; $\mathbf{Z} = (\mathrm{I}(X_1 \ge 0), \ldots, \mathrm{I}(X_N \ge 0))$ is a function of $\mathbf{X}$; the population, the bandwidth $b$ and the potential outcomes are fixed. The paper does not say where the potential outcomes take values; the validators take real numbers. (R2) $\mathrm{I}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function. $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\cdot)$ is the support of a discrete random vector, the set of its values of positive probability; the validators read a sum over $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})$ as a sum over distinct treatment vectors, each counted once (a set, not a multiset of running-variable arrangements). (R3) Because $\Pr(X_i \in W_0) \in \{0, 1\}$ for every $i$, the set of window subjects $S = \{i : \Pr(X_i \in W_0) = 1\}$ is nonrandom and $N_0 = |S|$ with probability one; the paper's sums over ‘$i : X_i \in W_0$’ are sums over $i \in S$. (R4) Notation used in the targets and not printed in the paper (the validators' notation; definitions, not extra assumptions): $S$ as in (R3); $n = |S| = N_0$; $m$, the number of window subjects treated; $p(\mathbf{z}) = \Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$; $\mathbf{X}_S = (X_i)_{i \in S}$; $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$, the $i$th component of $\mathbf{Y}$ (the paper uses $Y_i$ in the display for $\hat\tau$ without a separate definition). (R5) ‘The assumption of local randomization’ invoked on p. 131 is the p. 130 passage quoted above. It has formal clauses, stated for the full vector $\mathbf{X}$, and a prose consequence after the colon (all permutations of the running variable values within the window are equiprobable). Finding P014-E002 shows that the clauses do not imply the prose (P014-T5); the counterexamples to the unbiasedness display (P014-T1, P014-T9) satisfy both. (R6) In every counterexample the printed no-ties clause is read for distinct subjects, as its explanatory words ‘no two observed age values’ say; read literally (with $j = i$ allowed) no law satisfies it (finding P014-E003, P014-T7).
Scope of the list. Five confirmed errors change a mathematical statement or a formula and are targets: P014-E001 (Moderate; the individual average potential outcome is printed without assignment probabilities, and unbiasedness fails for the printed target), P014-E002 (Minor; the probability clause of the local randomization assumption is printed for the full vector $\mathbf{X}$), P014-E003 (Minor; the no-ties quantifier lacks $i \ne j$), P014-N004 (Minor; the summand of the display defining $\tau$ is not bracketed) and P014-N002 (Minor; the stated equivalence to Hudgens and Halloran's average direct effect, an interpretive finding that rests on an exact counterexample and on a sign). P014-E004 and P014-N006 are misprints in the reference list and are not targets. P014-N001 is undetermined, and P014-N003 and P014-N005 are not confirmed; none is a target. Of the five headline claims, P014-H1 is the unbiasedness statement (P014-T1 to P014-T4) and P014-H2 is the equivalence to Hudgens and Halloran's average direct effect (P014-T9, P014-T10). P014-H3 and P014-H5 are interpretive remarks. P014-H4 is the inference paragraph of pp. 131–132, which names sufficient regimes ‘given ... suitable regularity conditions’ and refers to Liu and Hudgens (2014) and Aronow and Samii (2016) for details: the note states no theorem, no asymptotic sequence and no conditions that could be transcribed, the cited works are not staged, and the one candidate about it (P014-N005) is not confirmed, so it is not a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2, the individual average potential outcome, the target $\tau$ and the unbiasedness display, corrected: probability-weighted averages, same estimator
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected definition and identity. The correction inserts $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$ in every summand of the numerator and of the denominator of the first display of p. 131; the estimator and the design are unchanged. From Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P014-E001, smallest_repair and prior_correction.corrected_text) and the validators' derivations (v1 derivation.md, ‘Why linearity instead gives the weighted target’; v2 derivation.md, section 5).] [Setting] A finite population of $N \ge 1$ subjects; for each subject $i$ a fixed function $y_i : \{0,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$, with no restriction (arbitrary interference); a random vector $\mathbf{Z}$ with values in $\{0,1\}^N$ and $p(\mathbf{z}) = \Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$; observed outcomes $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. A fixed set $S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ (the window subjects, $S = \{i : X_i \in W_0\}$) with $n = |S| = N_0$, and an integer $m$ with $0 < m < n$. [Hypotheses] (A1) $\sum_{i \in S} Z_i = m$ with probability one. (A2) $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = m/n$ for every $i \in S$. Nothing is assumed about $Z_j$ for $j \notin S$, nor about their dependence on $(Z_i)_{i \in S}$. [Corrected definitions] For $i \in S$ and $a \in \{0, 1\}$, $$\overline{Y}_i(a) = \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} p(\mathbf{z})\,y_i(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(z_i = a)}{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} p(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(z_i = a)} = \mathrm{E}[y_i(\mathbf{Z}) \mid Z_i = a],$$ where the denominator is $\Pr(Z_i = a)$, equal to $m/n$ for $a = 1$ and to $(n - m)/n$ for $a = 0$, hence positive; $$\tau = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in S}\bigl[\overline{Y}_i(1) - \overline{Y}_i(0)\bigr], \qquad \hat\tau = \frac{\sum_{i \in S} Y_iZ_i}{\sum_{i \in S} Z_i} - \frac{\sum_{i \in S} Y_i(1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i \in S}(1 - Z_i)}.$$ [Conclusion] $$\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \tau = \frac{1}{n}\left[\sum_{i \in S}\overline{Y}_i(1) - \sum_{i \in S}\overline{Y}_i(0)\right].$$ [Proof, each step part of the target.] (1) By (A1), with probability one $\hat\tau = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i \in S} y_i(\mathbf{Z})Z_i - \frac{1}{n - m}\sum_{i \in S} y_i(\mathbf{Z})(1 - Z_i)$. (2) For each $i \in S$, $\mathrm{E}[y_i(\mathbf{Z})Z_i] = \sum_{\mathbf{z}} p(\mathbf{z})\,y_i(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(z_i = 1) = \Pr(Z_i = 1)\,\overline{Y}_i(1) = \frac{m}{n}\overline{Y}_i(1)$, by the definition of $\overline{Y}_i(1)$ and (A2). (3) Likewise $\mathrm{E}[y_i(\mathbf{Z})(1 - Z_i)] = \sum_{\mathbf{z}} p(\mathbf{z})\,y_i(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(z_i = 0) = \Pr(Z_i = 0)\,\overline{Y}_i(0) = \frac{n - m}{n}\overline{Y}_i(0)$. (4) By linearity of expectation, $\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \frac{1}{m}\cdot\frac{m}{n}\sum_{i \in S}\overline{Y}_i(1) - \frac{1}{n - m}\cdot\frac{n - m}{n}\sum_{i \in S}\overline{Y}_i(0) = \tau$. [Under the corrected local randomization assumption.] If the running variables satisfy the corrected assumption of P014-T6 (the in-window subvector $\mathbf{X}_S$ is uniform over the $n!$ arrangements of $n$ fixed distinct values of which exactly $m$ are nonnegative, $0 < m < n$, and $Z_i = \mathrm{I}(X_i \ge 0)$), then (A1) and (A2) hold by P014-T6 (a) and (b), and therefore $\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \tau$ for arbitrary potential outcomes, whatever the allocation of the subjects outside $W_0$ and however it depends on the in-window arrangement.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Potential outcomes, assignment, observed outcomes: p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] $y_i(\mathbf{z})$, fixed, defined for all $\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^N$; $\mathbf{Z}$ a binary random vector of length $N$; $\mathbf{Y} = (y_1(\mathbf{Z}), \ldots, y_N(\mathbf{Z}))$, so $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. [Threshold rule: p. 130] $Z_i = 1$ if $X_i \geq 0$, else $Z_i = 0$. [Window: p. 130] $W_0 = [-b, b]$; $F_{\mathbf{x},W_0}$ is the empirical distribution function of $X_i$ for all subjects such that $X_i \in W_0$; $N_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{I}(X_i \in W_0)$. [Support and indicator: standing remark (R2)] $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})$ is the set of distinct vectors $\mathbf{z}$ with $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) > 0$; $\mathrm{I}(\cdot)$ is the indicator. [Estimator: p. 131 (PDF p. 4)] $$\hat\tau = \frac{\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Y_iZ_i}{\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Z_i} - \frac{\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Y_i(1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}(1 - Z_i)}.$$ with ‘$i : X_i \in W_0$’ written $i \in S$ (standing remark (R3)). On $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})$ its two denominators are $m$ and $n - m$ by (A1), so $\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} p(\mathbf{z})\,\hat\tau(\mathbf{z})$ is a finite sum of well-defined terms. [Not printed; validators' notation] $p(\mathbf{z}) = \Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$; $S$, $n$, $m$ as in standing remark (R4); $z_i$ is the $i$th component of $\mathbf{z}$. [What is replaced: p. 131] the printed display $$\overline{Y}_i(z) = \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} y_i(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{z}_i = z)}{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{z}_i = z)}.$$ and the printed target $$\tau = N_0^{-1}\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(1) - \overline{Y}_i(0).$$
canonical_claim.note: Repair cost recorded by Sol: different_estimand. The correction changes the target, not the estimator or the intended design; it adds no restriction on the allocation outside the window. In the witness of P014-T1 the target changes from $-1/18$ to $0$; in the second validator's witness from $4/3$ to $1$. Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P014-E001, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim: ‘Let S be fixed, n=|S|, 0<m<n, sum_{i in S} Z_i=m almost surely, and Pr(Z_i=1)=m/n for each i in S. For p(z)=Pr(Z=z) and fixed potential outcomes, define Ybar_i(a)=sum_z p(z)y_i(z)1{z_i=a}/sum_z p(z)1{z_i=a}. Define tau=n^{-1}sum_{i in S}(Ybar_i(1)-Ybar_i(0)). Then the unchanged difference-in-means estimator is unbiased for tau. Uniform local running-variable permutations ensure the fixed count and common propensities. Uniformity of full Z on its support, with these hypotheses, also permits retaining the original unweighted definition.’ The last sentence of that text is P014-T3. The corrected target is the one the paper's prose describes (‘the average outcome we would expect to see in treated subjects (across all subjects within the window and across all randomizations)’, p. 131), but the validators record that the context does not settle whether missing weights or a missing uniformity assumption was intended (intended_meaning_clear_from_context is false). The bracketing of the summand of $\tau$ is the correction of P014-N004 (P014-T8). Hypotheses (A1) and (A2) do not follow from the printed formal clauses of p. 130 alone (P014-T5); they follow from the corrected assumption (P014-T6). The derivation is given in both validators' artifacts (v1 and v2) in the same four steps; the path given is v2, section 5.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2, the display defining the target $\tau$, corrected: the summand bracketed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: p. 131 (PDF p. 4)] “Then our primary target is the average direct effect (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008) of treatment for subjects who are close to the threshold: $$\tau = N_0^{-1}\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(1) - \overline{Y}_i(0).$$” [Corrected; Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P014-N004)] $$\tau = N_0^{-1}\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\bigl[\overline{Y}_i(1) - \overline{Y}_i(0)\bigr].$$ [Mathematical content.] Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set with $n = |S|$ and let $u_i, w_i$ ($i \in S$) be real numbers. Then $$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in S}\bigl[u_i - w_i\bigr] = \frac{1}{n}\left[\sum_{i \in S} u_i - \sum_{i \in S} w_i\right].$$ With $S = \{i : X_i \in W_0\}$, $n = N_0$, $u_i = \overline{Y}_i(1)$ and $w_i = \overline{Y}_i(0)$, the corrected $\tau$ is equal to the right-hand side of the paper's later display $\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \frac{1}{N_0}\left[\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(1) - \sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(0)\right]$, so that display states $\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \tau$ for the corrected $\tau$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$\overline{Y}_i(z)$: p. 131 (PDF p. 4)] the individual average potential outcome; the identity holds for any real numbers, so it applies both to the printed definition $$\overline{Y}_i(z) = \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} y_i(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{z}_i = z)}{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{z}_i = z)}.$$ and to the probability-weighted definition of P014-T2. [$N_0$: p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] $N_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{I}(X_i \in W_0)$, the number of window subjects, positive under $0 < \sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Z_i < N_0$. [Later display: p. 131] $$\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \frac{1}{N_0}\left[\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(1) - \sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(0)\right],$$
canonical_claim.note: P014-N004 is rated an error, Minor: missing brackets in a display with one sensible reading. It is a target because the correction changes a printed formula and the author's instruction covers every mathematical error. The validator gives no numerical counterexample and none is needed: under the narrow-scope parse the last index $i$ is free and the factor $N_0^{-1}$ does not reach the control term, so the unbracketed display is not a well-formed definition (mathematical_checks.md, P014-N004). This target is about the grouping only. Whether $\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau]$ equals the bracketed $\tau$ depends on which $\overline{Y}_i$ is used: it fails for the printed unweighted averages (P014-T1) and holds for the probability-weighted ones (P014-T2).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2, the unbiasedness display with the printed (unweighted) target retained, corrected by an added condition on the assignment law
canonical_claim.statement: [Alternative correction: keep the printed definition of $\overline{Y}_i(z)$ and add an assumption under which it is the right target. From Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P014-E001, second alternative) and the validators' derivations (v1 derivation.md, ‘Alternative repair retaining the printed target’; v2 derivation.md, section 6).] [Setting] As in P014-T2: fixed $y_i : \{0,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$; $\mathbf{Z}$ random in $\{0,1\}^N$ with $p(\mathbf{z}) = \Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$; $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$; fixed $S$ with $n = |S|$; integer $0 < m < n$; (A1) $\sum_{i \in S} Z_i = m$ with probability one; (A2) $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = m/n$ for every $i \in S$; $\hat\tau$ the difference in means over $S$. For $i \in S$ and $a \in \{0,1\}$ write $K_{i,a} = \{\mathbf{z} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z}) : z_i = a\}$, nonempty by (A2), and let the printed average be $$\overline{Y}^{\mathrm{pr}}_i(a) = \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} y_i(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(z_i = a)}{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} \mathrm{I}(z_i = a)} = \frac{1}{|K_{i,a}|}\sum_{\mathbf{z} \in K_{i,a}} y_i(\mathbf{z}).$$ [Added condition (U)] For every $i \in S$ and $a \in \{0,1\}$, the conditional law of $\mathbf{Z}$ given $Z_i = a$ is uniform on its support: $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z} \mid Z_i = a) = 1/|K_{i,a}|$ for every $\mathbf{z} \in K_{i,a}$. [Claims] (a) Under (U), $\overline{Y}^{\mathrm{pr}}_i(a) = \mathrm{E}[y_i(\mathbf{Z}) \mid Z_i = a]$ for every $i \in S$, every $a$ and every choice of potential outcomes; hence under (A1), (A2) and (U) the printed identity holds: $$\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \frac{1}{n}\left[\sum_{i \in S}\overline{Y}^{\mathrm{pr}}_i(1) - \sum_{i \in S}\overline{Y}^{\mathrm{pr}}_i(0)\right].$$ (b) (U) holds whenever $\mathbf{Z}$ is uniform on $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})$. (c) [Fixed outside assignments.] Suppose $Z_j$ is almost surely constant for every $j \notin S$, $\mathbf{X}_S$ is uniform over the $n!$ arrangements of $n$ fixed distinct values of which exactly $m$ are nonnegative, and $Z_i = \mathrm{I}(X_i \ge 0)$. Then each binary vector on $S$ with exactly $m$ ones has $m!\,(n - m)!$ arrangements above it, $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})$ has $\binom{n}{m}$ points, each of probability $m!\,(n - m)!/n! = 1/\binom{n}{m}$, so $\mathbf{Z}$ is uniform on its support, (A1), (A2) and (U) hold, and the printed identity holds. (d) [No interference.] If for every $i \in S$ the potential outcome depends on $\mathbf{z}$ only through $z_i$ (that is, $y_i(\mathbf{z}) = y_i(\mathbf{z}')$ whenever $z_i = z'_i$), then under (A1) and (A2) alone, without (U), $\overline{Y}^{\mathrm{pr}}_i(a) = \mathrm{E}[y_i(\mathbf{Z}) \mid Z_i = a]$, both being the common value of $y_i$ on $\{\mathbf{z} : z_i = a\}$, and the printed identity holds. (e) [(U) is what the printed definition needs; v2 derivation.md, section 6.] Fix $i \in S$ and $a \in \{0,1\}$. If $\overline{Y}^{\mathrm{pr}}_i(a) = \mathrm{E}[y_i(\mathbf{Z}) \mid Z_i = a]$ for every function $y_i : \{0,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$, then $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z} \mid Z_i = a) = 1/|K_{i,a}|$ for every $\mathbf{z} \in K_{i,a}$ (take $y_i$ equal to one at a single point of $K_{i,a}$ and zero elsewhere).

canonical_claim.note: The second of the two repairs Sol records for P014-E001; it keeps the printed target and restricts the assignment law, where P014-T2 keeps the law and changes the target. The rating relies on it when it says the printed display ‘is already right when the full assignment is uniform on its support (fixed outside assignments, or no interference)’. Condition (U) is not supplied by the paper: it does not follow from the printed clauses or from equiprobable in-window permutations (P014-T1 has both and violates (U)), and requiring it limits the allocation outside the window that p. 131 says is ‘left completely unspecified’. canonical_claim.statement: [Introduction, p. 129 (PDF p. 2)] “We show that under a local randomization assumption, the difference-in-means estimator as applied to subjects in the window near the cutoff is unbiased for a regime-specific causal effect.” [Assumptions, p. 130 (PDF p. 3)] “To simplify our definition of local randomization, without loss of generality, assume that $\Pr(X_i = X_j) = 0, \forall i, j : X_i, X_j \in W_0$, so that no two observed age values within the window are exactly identical.” “Our local randomization assumption requires that $F_{\mathbf{x},W_0}(t) = F_0(t), \forall \mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$ and $\forall t$; $\Pr(X_i \in W_0) \in \{0, 1\}, \forall i \in \{1, ..., N\}$, $\Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{N_0!}, \forall \mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$, where $N_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{I}(X_i \in W_0)$: implying that all permutations of the running variable values (and therefore treatment values) within the window $W_0$ are equiprobable. Further assume that $0 < \sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Z_i < N_0$, so that at least one subject within the window is treated, and at least one subject within the window is in the control group.” [Estimands, p. 131 (PDF p. 4)] “We now define our causal estimands. Denote the individual average potential outcome under treatment $z$ for all subjects $i : X_i \in W_0$, $$\overline{Y}_i(z) = \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} y_i(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{z}_i = z)}{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{z}_i = z)}.$$ Note that this estimand is regime specific: it generally depends on the joint distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$. Depending on the treatment allocation scheme, then the individual average potential outcome would change. (E.g., when 90% of subjects in the population are treated, then both $\overline{Y}_i(0)$ and $\overline{Y}_i(1)$ might be different from when 10% of subjects in the population are treated.) While the treatment allocation scheme for subjects outside of $W_0$ is left completely unspecified, the allocation scheme for these subjects nevertheless contributes to the definition of each $\overline{Y}_i(z)$. Individual average potential outcomes marginalize over the treatment assignments for all units, not simply those within the window near the threshold.” “Then our primary target is the average direct effect (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008) of treatment for subjects who are close to the threshold: $$\tau = N_0^{-1}\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(1) - \overline{Y}_i(0).$$ Or, put simply, our target is the difference between the average outcome we would expect to see in treated subjects (across all subjects within the window and across all randomizations) and the average outcome we would expect to see in control subjects (across all subjects within the window and across all randomizations). When there is interference between subjects, this estimand is conditional not only on the subjects being close to the threshold in the running variable, but also on the exact way in which the treatment is assigned to all subjects in the finite population $U$.” [Result, p. 131 (PDF p. 4)] “We now show that $\tau$ is estimable and that the difference-in-means estimator as applied to all subjects $i : X_i \in W_0$ is unbiased for the average direct effect $\tau$ among these subjects. Formally, the difference-in-means estimator for subjects local to the threshold, $$\hat\tau = \frac{\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Y_iZ_i}{\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Z_i} - \frac{\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0} Y_i(1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}(1 - Z_i)}.$$ Then, under the assumption of local randomization, the difference-in-means estimator as applied to subjects local to the threshold is unbiased for the average direct effect for subjects near the threshold: $$\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \frac{1}{N_0}\left[\sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(1) - \sum_{i:X_i\in W_0}\overline{Y}_i(0)\right],$$ where the result trivially follows from linearity of expectations.”

The corresponding $\mathbf{Z}$ is $(1,0,0,1)$, $(0,1,0,1)$, and $(0,0,1,1)$ for each of the last four. [Claims] (i) [Every printed clause holds.] $\Pr(X_i \in W_0) = 1$ for $i = 1, 2, 3$ and $\Pr(X_4 \in W_0) = 0$, so $S = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $N_0 = 3$; for every $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$ the in-window values are $-2, -1, 1$ in some order, so $F_{\mathbf{x},W_0} = F_0$, the empirical distribution function of $\{-2, -1, 1\}$, at every $t$; $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$ has six points and $\Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = 1/6 = 1/N_0!$ at each; $\Pr(X_i = X_j) = 0$ for distinct $i, j \in S$; $\sum_{i \in S} Z_i = 1$ at every support point, so $0 < \sum_{i:X_i \in W_0} Z_i < N_0$. (ii) [The in-window permutations are not equiprobable.] $\Pr(\mathbf{X}_S = (1,-1,-2)) = 1/6$, $\Pr(\mathbf{X}_S = (-1,1,-2)) = 1/6$, $\Pr(\mathbf{X}_S = (-1,-2,1)) = 2/3$, and the other three arrangements of $(-2, -1, 1)$ have probability zero. On every support point one window subject is treated and $\hat\tau = Z_1$, so $\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = \Pr(Z_1 = 1) = 1/6 \ne 1/3 = \tau$.

canonical_claim.note: P014-E002 is rated an error, Minor. The brief's priority scale has no level for the counterexample of a Minor finding; 3 is used, as for its corrected statement (P014-T6) and as in other works of this audit. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Introduction and Section 2: the equivalence to Hudgens and Halloran (2008)’s average direct effect, corrected: probability-weighted individual averages, equal up to the sign convention
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected claim. From Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P014-N002, smallest_repair as settled by the external check), verbatim: ‘Replace the support-uniform display by \overline Y_i(z)=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\operatorname{Supp}(\mathbf Z):a_i=z} y_i(\mathbf a)\Pr(\mathbf Z=\mathbf a\mid Z_i=z), and identify the treated-minus-control window average as using the reverse of Hudgens–Halloran's sign convention.’] [Mathematical content, with every hypothesis.] Let $y_i : \{0,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ be fixed, $\mathbf{Z}$ a random vector in $\{0,1\}^N$ with $p(\mathbf{z}) = \Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$, and $S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ a fixed nonempty set with $n = |S| = N_0$ such that $0 < \Pr(Z_i = 1) < 1$ for every $i \in S$. For $i \in S$ and $s \in \{0,1\}$ define, in Hudgens and Halloran's form, $$m_i(s; p) = \sum_{\mathbf{u} \in \{0,1\}^{N-1}} y_i(s, \mathbf{u})\,\Pr(\mathbf{Z}_{-i} = \mathbf{u} \mid Z_i = s), \qquad d_i(p) = m_i(0; p) - m_i(1; p),$$ where $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ is $\mathbf{Z}$ with its $i$th component removed and $y_i(s, \mathbf{u})$ is $y_i$ at the vector with $i$th component $s$ and remaining components $\mathbf{u}$. (a) [The corrected individual average is Hudgens and Halloran's.] For every $i \in S$ and $s \in \{0,1\}$, $$m_i(s; p) = \sum_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z}):\,a_i = s} y_i(\mathbf{a})\,\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{a} \mid Z_i = s) = \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} p(\mathbf{z})\,y_i(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(z_i = s)}{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{Z})} p(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{I}(z_i = s)} = \mathrm{E}[y_i(\mathbf{Z}) \mid Z_i = s],$$ which is the corrected $\overline{Y}_i(s)$ of P014-T2. (b) [Equal up to sign.] With the corrected target $\tau = n^{-1}\sum_{i \in S}[\overline{Y}_i(1) - \overline{Y}_i(0)]$ of P014-T2, $$\tau = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in S} d_i(p):$$ the note's treated-minus-control target is the negative of the window average of Hudgens and Halloran's individual direct causal effect. (c) [Consequence for the estimator.] Under hypotheses (A1) and (A2) of P014-T2, $\mathrm{E}\,[\hat\tau] = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in S} d_i(p)$. (d) [The printed definition does not give this.] For the printed unweighted $\overline{Y}_i(s)$ the equality in (a) fails in general, and the printed $\tau$ equals neither $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in S} d_i(p)$ nor its negative: P014-T9.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2, the local randomization assumption, corrected: the probability clause stated for the in-window subvector
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected assumption. The correction replaces the clause ‘$\Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) =  rac{1}{N_0!},  orall \mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$’ by the same condition on the in-window subvector; the other clauses are kept. From Sol's smallest repair and corrected text (validated.json, P014-E002) and the validator's derivation (v1 derivation.md, sections 4 and 5).] Sol's corrected text, verbatim: ‘Let $S$ be the fixed set of local subjects, $n=|S|=N_0$, and let $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ be the fixed distinct local running-variable values. Replace the full-vector mass clause by $\Pr(\mathbf X_S=a)=1/n!$ for every permutation $a$ of these values. Require exactly $m$ nonnegative local values, with $0<m<n$, and set $Z_i=\mathbf1\{X_i\geq0\}$. Leave the conditional outside law unrestricted subject to fixed window membership. No independence between local and outside assignments is required. Then $\Pr(Z_i=1)=m/n$ for every $i\in S$.’ [Mathematical content, with every hypothesis.] Let $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_N)$ be a real random vector, $b > 0$, $W_0 = [-b, b]$, and $Z_i = \mathrm{I}(X_i \ge 0)$. Let $S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ with $n = |S| \ge 2$, and let $v_1, \ldots, v_n \in W_0$ be fixed distinct real numbers of which exactly $m$ are nonnegative, $0 < m < n$. Hypotheses: (L1) [fixed membership] $\Pr(X_i \in W_0) = 1$ for $i \in S$ and $\Pr(X_i \in W_0) = 0$ for $i 
otin S$. (L2) [uniform in-window arrangement] $\Pr(\mathbf{X}_S = \mathbf{a}) = 1/n!$ for each of the $n!$ arrangements $\mathbf{a}$ of $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ over the subjects in $S$, where $\mathbf{X}_S = (X_i)_{i \in S}$. Nothing is assumed about the conditional law of $(X_j)_{j 
otin S}$ given $\mathbf{X}_S$ beyond (L1); in particular no independence between the in-window and the outside running variables. Conclusions: (a) $\sum_{i \in S} Z_i = m$ with probability one, so $0 < \sum_{i \in S} Z_i < n$. (b) For every $i \in S$, $\Pr(Z_i = 1) =  rac{m\,(n-1)!}{n!} =  rac{m}{n}$ and $\Pr(Z_i = 0) =  rac{n - m}{n}$: there are $m$ choices of a nonnegative value for subject $i$ and $(n-1)!$ arrangements of the remaining values. (c) [The retained clauses hold.] With probability one $N_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{I}(X_i \in W_0) = n$ and the empirical distribution function of the in-window values is $F_0(t) = n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathrm{I}(v_k \le t)$; and $\Pr(X_i = X_j) = 0$ for all distinct $i, j \in S$. (d) [Why the printed clause is replaced and not added.] Suppose (L1) and (L2) hold and in addition the printed clause holds: $\mathbf{X}$ is discrete (as the paper's use of $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$ presupposes) and $\Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = 1/n!$ for every $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$. Then for each arrangement $\mathbf{a}$ there is exactly one $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$ with $\mathbf{x}_S = \mathbf{a}$; that is, $(X_j)_{j 
otin S}$ is, with probability one, a function of $\mathbf{X}_S$. Conversely, if (L1) and (L2) hold and $(X_j)_{j 
otin S} = g(\mathbf{X}_S)$ with probability one for some function $g$, then $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$ has $n!$ points, each of probability $1/n!$. (e) [A law that the corrected assumption admits and the printed clause excludes; validator's Part C.] $N = 4$, $b = 2$, $S = \{1, 2, 3\}$, $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$ a uniformly random arrangement of $(-2, -1, 1)$ and, independently, $X_4 = -3$ with probability $1/3$ and $X_4 = 3$ with probability $2/3$. Then (L1) and (L2) hold with $n = 3$, $m = 1$, while $\mathrm{Supp}\,(\mathbf{X})$ has 12 points, six of probability $1/18$ and six of probability $1/9$, none of probability $1/3! = 1/6$.

canonical_claim.note: P014-E002 is rated an error, Minor; repair cost recorded by Sol: none (the correction states formally the law that the paper's own prose describes; it changes neither the estimator nor the intended target). Conclusions (a) and (b) are hypotheses (A1) and (A2) of P014-T2, so this target and P014-T2 together give unbiasedness of the difference in means for the probability-weighted target under the corrected assumption. The correction does not by itself repair the printed unweighted target (P014-T1 satisfies (L1) and (L2)).
